summary.text: Factoring the factorial ratios into binomial coefficients, the proof obtains a cubic Kazandzidis congruence from harmonic-sum cancellations; a Dwork integrality criterion, a split into indices divisible and not divisible by powers of \(p\), and carry-counting estimates for the resulting tuple sums then yield coefficientwise divisibility by \(p^{3r}\). The exceptional cases \(m=1,2\) are reduced to the closed forms \(\tfrac12\binom{2N}{N}\) and \(\tfrac12\binom{4N}{N}\), respectively, and follow from the same binomial congruence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c_m(k)=\frac{(mk)!}{(k!)^m}\qquad (m,k\geq 0)
\]
and
\[
 L_{m,t}(x)=\sum_{k\geq1}\frac{c_m(kt)}{k}x^k,
 \qquad E_{m,t,N}(x)=\exp\bigl(NL_{m,t}(x)\bigr).
\]
Thus the series in the question is \(A_m(x)=E_{m,1,1}(x)\), and
\[
 A_m(x)^N=E_{m,1,N}(x).
\]
We prove that all coefficients of every \(E_{m,t,N}\) are nonnegative integers, and then prove
\[
 [x^{np^r}]E_{m,1,np^r}(x)\equiv
 [x^{np^{r-1}}]E_{m,1,np^{r-1}}(x)\pmod {p^{3r}}.                 \tag{1}
\]
Here \(m,n,r\geq1\) and \(p\geq5\) is prime.

Throughout the proof, \(v_p\) denotes the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on nonzero rationals, with \(v_p(0)=+\infty\). We write \(v_p(q)\geq a\) in the evident sense, also when \(a\) is negative. We repeatedly use the elementary rules
\[
\begin{aligned}
 v_p(a+b)&\geq\min(v_p(a),v_p(b)),\\
 v_p(ab)&=v_p(a)+v_p(b),\\
 v_p(1/u)&=-v_p(u)\quad(u\in\mathbb N,\ u>0).
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{2}
\]
For an integer \(z\), the assertion \(v_p(z)\geq s\), with \(s\geq0\), is equivalent to \(p^s\mid z\).

We first establish the arithmetic and power-series ingredients needed in the proof.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Formal exponentials
--------------------------------------------------------------------

If \(F(x)=\sum_{j\geq1}f_jx^j\) has zero constant term, define \(\exp(F)\) as the unique series \(G(x)=\sum_{k\geq0}g_kx^k\) satisfying
\[
 g_0=1,\qquad
 (k+1)g_{k+1}=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(j+1)f_{j+1}g_{k-j}.                 \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, (3) determines the coefficients successively, and it is exactly the coefficient form of
\[
 G'=F'G,\qquad G(0)=1.
\]
Uniqueness immediately gives
\[
 \exp(F+H)=\exp(F)\exp(H),\qquad \exp(NF)=\exp(F)^N.            \tag{4}
\]
If \(D_tF=F(x^t)\), the derivative recursion also shows
\[
 D_t(\exp F)=\exp(D_tF).                                       \tag{5}
\]
Finally, expanding the ordinary exponential and observing that \([x^k]F^\ell=0\) for \(\ell>k\), we have the finite formula
\[
 [x^k]\exp(F)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\frac{[x^k]F^\ell}{\ell!}.      \tag{6}
\]
All uses of exponentials below can therefore be justified purely by finite coefficient identities.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The factorial ratios and their valuations
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The number \(c_m(k)\) is an integer. In fact, by induction on \(m\),
\[
 (k!)^m\mid(mk)!,
\]
because \((mk)!k!\mid((m+1)k)!\). It is positive, and it also has the product representation
\[
 c_m(J)=\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\binom{(i+1)J}{J}.                    \tag{7}
\]
Let
\[
 \nu_m(k)=v_p(c_m(k)).
\]
Legendre’s formula yields, for any sufficiently large \(B\),
\[
 \nu_m(k)=\sum_{s=1}^{B-1}
 \left(\left\lfloor\frac{mk}{p^s}\right\rfloor
       -m\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p^s}\right\rfloor\right).       \tag{8}
\]
Every summand is nonnegative. Consequently, for every \(R\),
\[
 \nu_m(k)\geq\sum_{s=1}^{R}
 \left(\left\lfloor\frac{mk}{p^s}\right\rfloor
       -m\left\lfloor\frac{k}{p^s}\right\rfloor\right).       \tag{9}
\]
Legendre’s formula also directly gives
\[
 \nu_m(pJ)=\nu_m(J).                                           \tag{10}
\]
For later use, if \(p\geq5\) and \(\ell\geq1\), then
\[
 4v_p(\ell!)+1\leq\ell.                                       \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, if \(s_p(\ell)\) is the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(\ell\), then
\[
 (p-1)v_p(\ell!)=\ell-s_p(\ell),
\]
and \(s_p(\ell)\geq1\). Since \(p-1\geq4\), (11) follows.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Harmonic sums and the strengthened binomial congruence
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We require a precise version of the Jacobsthal–Kazandzidis congruence. We give its proof because the power \(p^{3r}\) in the final theorem comes from it.

For \(N>0\), put \(w=v_p(N)\), and sum only over integers \(0\leq k<N\) not divisible by \(p\). Then, for \(p\geq5\),
\[
 v_p\left(\sum_{\substack{0\leq k<N\\p\nmid k}}\frac1{k^2}\right)\geq w,               \tag{12}
\]
where the term \(k=0\) is absent automatically, and
\[
 v_p\left(\sum_{\substack{0\leq k<N\\p\nmid k}}\frac1k\right)\geq2w.                 \tag{13}
\]
If \(w=0\), these merely say that the sums are \(p\)-integral. Suppose \(w\geq1\). Set
\[
 e=(p-1)p^w-2.
\]
Euler’s theorem modulo \(p^{w+1}\) gives, for \(p\nmid k\),
\[
 k^{-2}\equiv k^e\pmod {p^{w+1}}.                              \tag{14}
\]
Faulhaber’s formula, written as
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}k^e
 =\sum_{i=0}^{e}\binom ei B_i\frac{N^{e+1-i}}{e+1-i},           \tag{15}
\]
shows that the full power sum has valuation at least \(w\). Here one uses the standard denominator consequence of the Bernoulli recursion: \(v_p(B_i)\geq-1\), and, if \(i>0\) and \((p-1)\nmid i\), then \(v_p(B_i)\geq0\). For completeness, the latter follows by comparing the Bernoulli recursion at \(p\) with the fact that \(\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}a^i=0\) when \((p-1)\nmid i\). Each term of (15) then has valuation at least \(w\); the last term uses \((p-1)\nmid e\), and the others use
\[
 v_p(d)+2\leq d\quad(d\geq2,\,p\geq3).
\]
The contribution from multiples of \(p\) is \(p^e\sum_{j<N/p}j^e\), also of valuation at least \(w\). Combining this with (14) proves (12).

To prove (13), pair \(k\) with \(N-k\). An exact algebraic identity is
\[
 \frac1k+\frac1{N-k}
 =-\frac{N}{k^2}-\frac{N^2}{k^3}
   -\frac{N^3}{k^3(k-N)}.                                      \tag{16}
\]
The first sum on the right has valuation at least \(w+w=2w\) by (12), and the other two have valuation at least \(2w\), because all displayed denominators are \(p\)-units. Since \(2\) is also a \(p\)-unit, (13) follows.

Now let \(b\geq1\), \(c\geq0\), and let \(v\) satisfy
\[
 v\leq v_p(bp),\qquad v_p(cp)\geq v.
\]
Then
\[
 v_p\left(
 \frac{\binom{(b+c)p}{bp}}{\binom{b+c}{b}}-1
 \right)\geq3v.                                                \tag{17}
\]
To prove this, split a factorial into its factors divisible by \(p\) and prime to \(p\). Cancellation gives
\[
 \frac{\binom{(b+c)p}{bp}}{\binom{b+c}{b}}
 =\prod_{\substack{1\leq j<bp\\p\nmid j}}
 \left(1+\frac{cp}{j}\right).                                 \tag{18}
\]
(The harmless endpoint convention in the product does not matter; the set is precisely the prime-to-\(p\) factors in a block of length \(bp\).)
Put \(y_j=cp/j\). Every \(y_j\) has valuation at least \(v\). Expanding the product through degree two gives
\[
 \prod_j(1+y_j)=1+\sum_jy_j+ rac{(\sum_jy_j)^2-\sum_jy_j^2}{2}+R,
\]
where every monomial in \(R\) has degree at least three and hence valuation at least \(3v\). By (13),
\[
 v_p\left(\sum_jy_j\right)
 \geq v+2v_p(bp)\geq3v.
\]
By (12),
\[
 v_p\left(\sum_jy_j^2\right)
 \geq2v+v_p(bp)\geq3v.
\]
The square of the first sum has still larger valuation, and division by \(2\) loses nothing. This proves (17).

Without using (12)–(13), (18) immediately gives the weaker but universally valid Gauss estimate
\[
 v_p\left(
 \frac{\binom{(b+c)p}{bp}}{\binom{b+c}{b}}-1
 \right)\geq v_p(cp).                                         \tag{19}
\]

Apply (17) factor by factor to (7). If \(J>0\), then
\[
 v_p\bigl(c_m(pJ)-c_m(J)\bigr)
 \geq \nu_m(J)+3+3v_p(J).                                     \tag{20}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 c_m(pJ)=c_m(J)\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}
 \frac{\binom{(J+iJ)p}{Jp}}{\binom{J+iJ}{J}},                  \tag{21}
\]
and each ratio differs from \(1\) by a number of valuation at least
\(3(1+v_p(J))\). Multiplying the product-minus-one by \(c_m(J)\) contributes \(\nu_m(J)\). The same argument using (19) gives, for every prime,
\[
 v_p\bigl(c_m(pJ)-c_m(J)\bigr)
 \geq \nu_m(J)+1+v_p(J).                                      \tag{22}
\]

A useful direct consequence of (17) is the following. For every \(i\geq0\), \(n,r\geq1\),
\[
 \binom{(1+i)np^r}{np^r}\equiv
 \binom{(1+i)np^{r-1}}{np^{r-1}}\pmod {p^{3r}}.                \tag{23}
\]
Take \(b=np^{r-1}\), \(c=ib\), and \(v=r\) in (17), then multiply the ratio-minus-one by the lower binomial coefficient, which is an integer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Integrality of the exponential series
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We use the following coefficient form of Dwork’s lemma.

**Dwork lemma.** If \(F(0)=0\) and every coefficient of
\[
 pF(x)-F(x^p)                                                    \tag{24}
\]
has valuation at least \(1\), then every coefficient of \(\exp(F)\) is \(p\)-integral.

Here is a proof. Put \(E=\exp(F)\), \(\Delta=pF-F(x^p)\). By (4)–(5),
\[
 E(x)^p=E(x^p)\exp(\Delta).                                    \tag{25}
\]
If a series has \(p\)-integral coefficients, its \(p\)-th power is coefficientwise congruent modulo \(p\) to the series obtained by replacing \(x\) by \(x^p\). This follows first for a polynomial by the binomial theorem, since \(p\mid\binom pt\) for \(0<t<p\), together with \(a^p\equiv a\pmod p\) for a \(p\)-integral rational \(a\); truncation proves the formal-series statement.

Induct on the coefficient index \(k\). Assume the coefficients of \(E\) below degree \(k\) are \(p\)-integral. Truncate \(E\) below degree \(k\). Comparing degree \(k\) in (25), and separating the occurrence of \([x^k]E\) in the left side, gives
\[
 p[x^k]E=(\text{a sum involving only lower coefficients of }E
          \text{ and positive-degree coefficients of }\exp\Delta)
 -[x^k](A^p-A(x^p)),                                            \tag{26}
\]
where \(A\) is the truncation below degree \(k\). Every positive-degree coefficient of \(\exp\Delta\) is divisible by \(p\): by (6), each nonconstant term contains at least one coefficient of \(\Delta\), while division by \(\ell!\) cannot erase all of that factor since \(v_p(\ell!)\leq\ell-1\). The last term of (26) is divisible by \(p\) by the Frobenius congruence. Thus the right side has valuation at least \(1\), proving that \([x^k]E\) is \(p\)-integral.

We apply the lemma to \(F=NL_{m,t}\), where \(t>0\). At an index \(j\) not divisible by \(p\), the coefficient of (24) is
\[
 \frac{pN c_m(jt)}j,
\]
which has valuation at least one. If \(j=pJ\), it is
\[
 \frac N J\bigl(c_m(pJt)-c_m(Jt)\bigr),
\]
which has valuation at least one by (22), because
\(v_p(J)\leq v_p(Jt)\) and \(\nu_m(Jt)\geq0\). Hence every coefficient of \(E_{m,t,N}\) is \(p\)-integral for every prime \(p\).

A rational number integral at every prime has denominator one: otherwise a prime divisor of its reduced denominator would give negative valuation. Thus every coefficient of \(E_{m,t,N}\) is an integer. Formula (3), or equivalently (6), also shows inductively that these coefficients are nonnegative, since all coefficients of \(NL_{m,t}\) are nonnegative. Therefore
\[
 [x^k]E_{m,t,N}(x)\in\mathbb N.                                \tag{27}
\]
This proves the integrality assertion needed in the conjecture.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Two carry inequalities
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The difficult coefficient comparison for \(m\geq3\) reduces to two combinatorial valuation inequalities. We prove them now.

Let \(S\geq1\), let \(d_t\) be finitely many positive integers whose sum is divisible by \(p^S\), and let
\[
 L_S=\#\{t:p^S\nmid d_t\}.
\]
If \(L_S>0\), then in fact \(L_S\neq1\): if exactly one summand were not divisible by \(p^S\), subtracting all the divisible summands from the divisible total would show that the remaining one was divisible too.

Define
\[
 \delta_S(d)=\left\lfloor\frac{md}{p^S}\right\rfloor
       -m\left\lfloor\frac d{p^S}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m(d\bmod p^S)}{p^S}\right\rfloor.          \tag{28}
\]
Then
\[
 m+1\leq L_S+\sum_t\delta_S(d_t)\qquad(L_S>0).                 \tag{29}
\]
To see this, put \(P=p^S\) and \(u_t=d_t\bmod P\). The positive sum \(\sum u_t\) is a multiple of \(P\), hence at least \(P\). Write
\[
 \sum_t(mu_t\bmod P)=\tau P.
\]
Only the \(L_S\) nonzero residues contribute, each by at most \(P-1\), so \(\tau+1\leq L_S\). On the other hand,
\[
 m\sum_tu_t=P\left(\sum_t\left\lfloor\frac{mu_t}{P}\right\rfloor+\tau\right)
 \geq mP,
\]
so \(m\leq\sum_t\delta_S(d_t)+\tau\). Combining these two inequalities proves (29).

If no \(d_t\) is divisible by \(p^R\), then counting, for each \(t\), the levels above \(v_p(d_t)\) gives
\[
 \sum_t(R-v_p(d_t))=\sum_{S=1}^{R}L_S.                         \tag{30}
\]
Combining (9), (29), (30), and (11) gives the following two estimates.

**F-inequality.** Suppose \(m\geq3\), \(R\geq1\), every \(d_t>0\), no \(d_t\) is divisible by \(p^R\), their sum is divisible by \(p^R\), and at least two of them are prime to \(p\). If there are \(\ell\) terms, then
\[
 3R+v_p(\ell!)
 \leq \sum_t(R-v_p(d_t))+\sum_t\nu_m(d_t).                    \tag{31}
\]
Indeed, the hypothesis gives \(L_S\geq2\) for all \(1\leq S\leq R\). Summing (29), using (9), gives at least \((R-1)(m+1)+\max(\ell,m+1)\): at the top level \(L_R=\ell\), while every level contributes at least \(m+1\). Since \(m+1\geq4\), (11) supplies the remaining elementary inequality needed to obtain (31). Explicitly, \(4(R-1)\leq(R-1)(m+1)\), \(4v_p(\ell!)+1\leq\ell\) when \(\ell>0\), and \(\max(\ell,m+1)\) dominates both \(\ell\) and \(m+1\).

**K-inequality.** Under the same assumptions at level \(R\), choose one distinguished term \(d_{t_0}\), and put \(a_0=v_p(d_{t_0})<R\). Then
\[
 3(R+1)+v_p(\ell!)
 \leq \sum_t(R-v_p(d_t))+\sum_t\nu_m(d_t)+3+3a_0.              \tag{32}
\]
For this, sum (29) only over \(S=a_0+1,\ldots,R\). At all these levels the distinguished term is nondivisible, so \(L_S>0\), and the preceding observation makes \(L_S\geq2\). The resulting lower bound is
\[
 (R-1-a_0)(m+1)+\max(\ell,m+1).
\]
The same use of \(m+1\geq4\) and (11), after moving the bonus \(3+3a_0\) to the right, gives (32). These arguments also cover \(\ell=0\), when \(v_p(0!)=0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The level correction series
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix \(p,m,n\). For \(\rho\geq0\), define
\[
 P_\rho(x)=\sum_{u\geq0}P_\rho(u)x^u,
 \qquad
 P_\rho(u)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&p^\rho\mid u,\\[2mm]
 \displaystyle\frac{np^\rho c_m(u)}u,&p^\rho\nmid u.
 \end{cases}                                                    \tag{33}
\]
In particular \(P_\rho(0)=0\). Splitting the indices according as \(p^\rho\mid u\) gives the exact identity
\[
 np^\rho L_{m,1}(x)=P_\rho(x)+nL_{m,p^\rho}(x^{p^\rho}).       \tag{34}
\]
Exponentiating,
\[
 E_{m,1,np^\rho}(x)
 =\exp(P_\rho(x))E_{m,p^\rho,n}(x^{p^\rho}).                  \tag{35}
\]

From (33), (2), and the definition of \(\nu_m\), if \(p^\rho\nmid u\),
\[
 v_p(P_\rho(u))\geq \rho-v_p(u)+\nu_m(u).                     \tag{36}
\]
If \(r\geq1\), \(p^{r-1}\nmid J\), then (10) gives
\[
 v_p(P_r(pJ))\geq r-1-v_p(J)+\nu_m(J),                         \tag{37}
\]
and (20) gives the stronger difference estimate
\[
 v_p\bigl(P_r(pJ)-P_{r-1}(J)\bigr)
 \geq r-1-v_p(J)+\nu_m(J)+3+3v_p(J).                           \tag{38}
\]
Indeed, after cancelling one factor \(p\), the difference is exactly
\[
 \frac{np^{r-1}}J\bigl(c_m(pJ)-c_m(J)\bigr).
\]

The coefficients of \(\exp(P_\rho)\) are \(p\)-integral. This follows directly from (35): both \(E_{m,1,np^\rho}\) and \(E_{m,p^\rho,n}\) have \(p\)-integral coefficients by (27), the latter has constant coefficient one, and recursive division of power series shows that the quotient of two such series is again \(p\)-integral. Thus
\[
 v_p([x^k]\exp(P_\rho))\geq0.                                 \tag{39}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Comparison of the correction exponentials for \(m\geq3\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We prove
\[
 v_p\left([x^{p^rj}]\exp(P_r)-[x^{p^{r-1}j}]\exp(P_{r-1})\right)
 \geq3r                                                     \tag{40}
\]
for every \(j\geq0\). The case \(j=0\) is immediate because both constant coefficients are one. Assume \(j>0\).

By (6), it is enough to prove, for every \(\ell\geq0\),
\[
 v_p\left([x^{p^rj}]P_r^\ell-[x^{p^{r-1}j}]P_{r-1}^\ell\right)
 \geq3r+v_p(\ell!).                                           \tag{41}
\]
Indeed, division by \(\ell!\) then leaves valuation at least \(3r\), and terms with \(\ell\) larger than the degree vanish.

Expand the first coefficient as a sum over ordered \(\ell\)-tuples
\((d_1,\ldots,d_\ell)\) with sum \(p^rj\), the summand being
\(\prod_tP_r(d_t)\). A summand vanishes if some \(p^r\mid d_t\), by (33), so retain only tuples with no such part. Split them into two classes.

First suppose at least two parts are prime to \(p\). By (36), the product has valuation at least
\[
 \sum_t\bigl(r-v_p(d_t)+\nu_m(d_t)\bigr).
\]
The F-inequality (31) says this is at least \(3r+v_p(\ell!)\). Thus the entire sum over this class has that valuation.

For the remaining tuples, all parts are divisible by \(p\). To justify this assertion, note that the number of prime-to-\(p\) parts cannot be exactly one: the total \(p^rj\) is divisible by \(p\), as are all other parts, forcing the exceptional part to be divisible by \(p\) as well. Dividing every part by \(p\) gives a bijection with the tuples \((e_1,\ldots,e_\ell)\) of sum \(p^{r-1}j\) for which no \(e_t\) is divisible by \(p^{r-1}\). Therefore the contribution still to be compared is a sum of
\[
 \prod_tP_r(pe_t)-\prod_tP_{r-1}(e_t).                         \tag{42}
\]
If \(r=1\), there are no such tuples, because every integer is divisible by \(p^0=1\). Suppose \(r\geq2\).

Use the telescoping product identity: a difference \(\prod a_t-\prod b_t\) is a sum in which one factor is \(a_t-b_t\), earlier factors are of type \(a\), and later factors of type \(b\). Set
\[
 w_t=r-1-v_p(e_t)+\nu_m(e_t),\qquad
 \delta_t=3+3v_p(e_t).
\]
By (36)–(38), both \(P_r(pe_t)\) and \(P_{r-1}(e_t)\) have valuation at least \(w_t\), while their difference has valuation at least \(w_t+\delta_t\). The K-inequality (32), with each possible distinguished index in turn, states
\[
 \sum_tw_t+\delta_t\geq3r+v_p(\ell!).
\]
Every term in the telescoping identity therefore has the required valuation. This proves (41), hence (40).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Comparison of the residual exponentials
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For every \(m\), not merely \(m\geq3\), we also have
\[
 v_p\left([x^i]E_{m,p^r,n}-[x^i]E_{m,p^{r-1},n}\right)\geq3r.  \tag{43}
\]
Put
\[
 D=nL_{m,p^r}-nL_{m,p^{r-1}}.
\]
Its constant coefficient is zero. For \(k>0\), put \(J=kp^{r-1}\). Its \(k\)-th coefficient is
\[
 \frac nk\bigl(c_m(pJ)-c_m(J)\bigr).
\]
By (20), and because
\(v_p(J)=v_p(k)+r-1\), this has valuation at least \(3r\). Thus every coefficient of \(D\) has valuation at least \(3r\). Formula (6), together with \(v_p(\ell!)\leq\ell-1\), implies that every positive-degree coefficient of \(\exp(D)-1\) also has valuation at least \(3r\). Since
\[
 E_{m,p^r,n}=E_{m,p^{r-1},n}\exp(D)
\]
and the coefficients of the first factor are \(p\)-integral by (27), convolution proves (43).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Completion for \(m\geq3\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Take the coefficient of degree \(np^\rho\) in (35). Since the second factor only has powers divisible by \(p^\rho\),
\[
 [x^{np^\rho}]E_{m,1,np^\rho}
 =\sum_{w=0}^{n}
 [x^{p^\rho(n-w)}]\exp(P_\rho)\,[x^w]E_{m,p^\rho,n}.           \tag{44}
\]
Subtract (44) at \(\rho=r-1\) from (44) at \(\rho=r\), term by term. For each \(w\), use
\[
 ab-cd=(a-c)b+c(b-d).
\]
The first difference \(a-c\) has valuation at least \(3r\) by (40), while \(b\) is \(p\)-integral by (27). The factor \(c\) is \(p\)-integral by (39), while \(b-d\) has valuation at least \(3r\) by (43). Hence every summand, and therefore their sum, has valuation at least \(3r\). This proves (1) for \(m\geq3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
10. The cases \(m=1\) and \(m=2\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

These two cases have simpler closed forms.

For \(m=1\), \(c_1(k)=1\), so
\[
 \exp(NL_{1,1}(x))=(1-x)^{-N}.
\]
Consequently, for \(M\geq1\),
\[
 [x^M]E_{1,1,M}=\binom{2M-1}{M}=\frac12\binom{2M}{M}.          \tag{45}
\]
Taking \(M=np^r\) and \(M=np^{r-1}\), congruence (23) with \(i=1\), followed by division by the \(p\)-unit \(2\), proves (1).

For \(m=2\), \(c_2(k)=\binom{2k}{k}\). Let
\[
 C(x)=\sum_{k\geq0}\frac1{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}x^k

after interpreting the displayed coefficients as the usual Catalan integers. The Catalan equation is
\[
 C=1+xC^2.                                                      \tag{46}
\]
A standard coefficient calculation from (46), or differentiation followed by coefficient comparison, gives
\[
 \exp(NL_{2,1}(x))=C(x)^{2N}.                                  \tag{47}
\]
For clarity, differentiating the logarithm of the right side gives
\(2N C'/C\); the Catalan equation implies that this equals
\(N(L_{2,1})'\), and both sides of (47) have constant coefficient one.

The ballot-number identity
\[
 [x^k]C(x)^j=\frac{j}{2k+j}\binom{2k+j}{k}

after the appropriate limiting interpretation at \(j=0\), or equivalently its elementary Pascal-recursion proof, gives at \(j=2M\), \(k=M\),
\[
 [x^M]E_{2,1,M}=[x^M]C^{2M}
 =\frac12\binom{4M}{M}.                                       \tag{48}
\]
Now use (23) with \(i=3\), again dividing by the \(p\)-unit \(2\). This proves (1) for \(m=2\).

Thus (1) holds for every positive \(m\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
11. Identification with the sequence in the statement
--------------------------------------------------------------------

It remains to connect the coefficients just used with the recursively defined integer sequence. If
\[
 \exp\left(\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{d_j}{j}x^j\right)
   =\sum_{k\geq0}a_kx^k,
\]
then (3) says
\[
 a_0=1,
 \qquad
 a_k=\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}d_j a_{k-j}.                         \tag{49}
\]
For \(A_m(x)^N=E_{m,1,N}(x)\), we have \(d_j=Nc_m(j)\). By (27), the right side of (49) is an integer. Hence the natural-number recursion used to define the sequence—namely, start with \(a_0=1\), form the indicated nonnegative integer sum, and divide by \(k\)—agrees, by induction on \(k\), with the coefficient of \(E_{m,1,N}\). In particular,
\[
 b_m(N)=[x^N]A_m(x)^N=[x^N]E_{m,1,N}(x)\in\mathbb Z.           \tag{50}
\]
Taking \(N=np^r\) and \(N=np^{r-1}\) in (50), congruence (1) says that their difference has \(p\)-adic valuation at least \(3r\). Since both are integers, this is exactly
\[
 b_m(np^r)\equiv b_m(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
This proves both the integrality of the associated coefficients and the asserted supercongruence for every positive \(m,n,r\) and every prime \(p\geq5\).
